8	> Development runs the production engine: same class, same direct method

24	boundary. Vue reconstructs the affected component and its setup-owned class
25	instance. When no narrower boundary can accept the update, Vite reloads the
26	page.

28	Every class edit follows that same coherent lifecycle:
29	
30	- method and getter edits;
31	- constructor and field edits;
32	- native `#private` edits;
33	- inheritance changes;
34	- added, removed, or renamed members.

40	## Template edits still preserve state
41	
42	Vue owns SFC template HMR. Editing only a template updates its render function
43	while Vue preserves component state where its normal HMR rules permit it.
44	
45	Editing the class or component script rebuilds the affected owner. This matches
46	the lifecycle developers already receive from ordinary Vue setup code:
47

49	template edit     → Vue updates rendering and preserves state
50	class/script edit → Vue reconstructs the affected owner
51	unsafe boundary   → Vite reloads the page
52	```

56	## Why reconstruction is the complete operation
57	
58	A class instance combines several kinds of generation-specific state:
59	
60	- field initializers and constructor side effects;
61	- cached refs, computeds, and singleton getters;
62	- bound method references;
63	- inheritance and `super` relationships;
64	- native private brands;
65	- watchers, listeners, and lifecycle registration.
66	
67	Replacing only prototype methods creates a hybrid object: old state and wiring
68	running new behavior. Supporting that hybrid requires a class registry,
69	construct proxy, live method slots, source signatures, edit classification,
70	collision handling, and remount escalation.
71	
72	Owner reconstruction applies the complete new declaration. It needs none of
73	that machinery and cannot silently retain an incompatible old fragment.

75	## Production parity
76	
77	`Reactive()` has one implementation across environments:
78	
79	| Property | Development | Test / SSR | Production |
80	|---|---|---|---|
81	| Returned constructor | input class | input class | input class |
82	| Construction | native `new` | native `new` | native `new` |
83	| Instance | plain object | plain object | plain object |
84	| Method binding | direct lazy bind | direct lazy bind | direct lazy bind |
85	| Class registry | none | none | none |
86	| Construct proxy | none | none | none |
87	| Live method slot | none | none | none |

91	Benchmarks run during development therefore exercise the same ivue class
92	semantics as a production build.

94	## Ownership determines the reload boundary
95	
96	A class constructed in component setup belongs to that component. Vue unmounts
97	the owner, runs its normal cleanup, and constructs the replacement.
98	
99	An instance that outlives components needs an explicit owner in ordinary code

104	let session = new Session.Class();

109	}
110	```

![Development should run production](/blog/hot-reload-for-logic.png)

Hot module replacement is seductive because every piece of state it preserves
feels like progress. That convenience has a price when a library must introduce
a different runtime to provide it.

A class-grafting engine needs a stable class registry, a construct proxy, live
method slots, source signatures, collision detection, private-brand detection,
and rules for deciding which edits can mutate a living object. Development then
runs through machinery production never executes.

ivue takes the smaller contract:

> Development executes the production engine. Vue owns the reconstruction
===MODULES===
leave a child class holding an old parent, or make a dependency read before its
replacement module has finished initializing. The namespace pattern removes
those eager class-value edges. Each module can re-evaluate, and the next late
`Other.Class` read reaches the coherent class graph Vite has just loaded.

That means ivue relies on **normal Vite replacement**, not a custom runtime
that grafts methods into live instances. A reload gives new construction and
future late reads the new classes. It deliberately does **not** promise to
mutate existing instances or preserve their local state across a class edit.
The benefit is one runtime model in development and production, with no
development-only class graph to maintain.

## Injecting stores and composables: the `$` slot

## Let Node own restart

Use the project's existing watcher to restart the process after edits. Do not
add module invalidation, donor generations, method grafting, callback
forwarding registries, or state migration to this pattern.

The namespace shape makes a clean restart dependable because cross-module
values resolve after initialization. Production and development execute the
same capability classes and selected methods.

===LESSONS===
- String processing on user source (hmrNormalize): a state-tracking scanner
  beats regex — the regex version collapsed whitespace **inside string
  literals**, silently corrupting semantics.
- **Native `#private` brands change on every class evaluation, even when the
  source is identical.** Class HMR must treat the presence of a native private
  member as rebuild-required and invalidate the owner boundary; grafting donor
  methods onto old branded instances throws. Source detection must ignore `#`
  inside strings, templates, comments, and regex literals.
- Production size gate: the engine is ~1.1 KB gzipped — re-verify the build
  size after any engine edit; DCE regressions are silent.

# Node Development by Restart

::: warning Current exploration
This page defines the development boundary for the experimental Node namespace
model. It is not an ivue package feature.

> A runtime should own only the problems the host runtime does not already

The Node namespace model solves authoring structure: circular dependencies
resolve late, static methods are passable, inheritance remains native, and
boot composition selects one class. A normal Node watcher already solves the
remaining development event by restarting the process after an edit.

```text
edit
→ watcher stops the process
→ Node loads one fresh module graph
→ namespaces compose
→ routes retain methods from that generation
→ application runs
```

Yes — and your instinct about *which part* is the invariant is exactly right. Let me reduce it cleanly:

**The invariant:** every visually-highlighted text role must carry a distinct signal — links (navigation), inline code (notation), buttons (action). Before the change, links and chips shared indigo: two different meanings, one signal. In these docs that collision was unusually expensive, because the prose is dense with inline code *and* many links wrap code chips — a reader had to parse context to know "clickable or notation?" Removing that ambiguity is structural, not taste: it survives theme changes (it lives in the tokens), it removes per-case judgment (any new surface just picks its color by role), and it generates correct expectations everywhere. That's invariant-shaped.

**Blue specifically is the expression, not the essence.** Any hue distinct from chip-violet and button-indigo would have satisfied the structure. But blue is the strongest possible expression of it, because "links are blue" is the oldest convention on the web — you inherit thirty years of trained intuition for free. So: *distinctness* is the invariant; *blue* is its canonical clothing.

**Purple buttons are fine — and the reduction says why.** Buttons don't need hue to carry their role, because they're disambiguated by a second channel: shape. A filled pill with white text can't be mistaken for a link or a chip regardless of its color. That frees the buttons to carry the *brand* (the indigo→emerald identity) rather than the role. Which is the tidy end state we landed on: hue distinguishes text roles where shape can't; shape distinguishes buttons, so their hue is free to do brand work.

And on Geist Mono feeling perfect — there's a structural reason for that too: it's the sibling of Geist, the body font. Code and prose now share one typographic family, so code blocks read as part of the page rather than a quotation from somewhere else. The tour through JetBrains/Fira/Source/Plex was worth it precisely because it proved the original pairing wasn't an accident.

import re, glob

    r'href="https://stackblitz\.com/github/infinite-system/ivue/tree/main/examples/playground\?([^"]*)"([^>]*)>'
)

def transform(match):
    query = match.group(1)
    params = dict(p.split('=', 1) for p in query.split('&') if '=' in p)
    file = params.get('file', '')
    path = params.get('initialPath') or params.get('initialpath') or ''
    href = '/examples/stackblitz'
    q = []
    if file: q.append('file=' + file)
    if path: q.append('path=' + path)
    if q: href += '?' + '&'.join(q)
    return f'href="{href}">'

changed = []
for f in glob.glob('docs_v2/examples/*.md'):
    if f.endswith('stackblitz.md'):
        continue
    s = open(f).read()
    new = pattern.sub(transform, s)
    if new != s:
        open(f, 'w').write(new)
        changed.append(f)
print('\n'.join(changed))
EOF

Diagnosed and fixed, committed as `d2f014d` (not pushed). What actually happened to you on the Advanced Select page:

**The failure chain.** During a Pages deploy there's a window where the old hashed asset files are already deleted but the new HTML hasn't propagated (Pages caches HTML for up to 10 minutes). Your tab requested the example's chunks (that page fires several dynamic imports at once — Quasar loader plus the example itself), got 404s, and the recovery script did its one cache-busted reload — which landed on *still-stale* HTML referencing the same dead chunks. The re-failure hit the script's one-shot session guard, whose behavior was literally `return;` — no retry, no poll, nothing. Stuck until your hard refresh.

**Three fixes, all verified against the production build with synthetic failure events:**

1. **The guard is now a 15-second timestamp instead of a one-shot** — recovery re-arms by itself, so a failure minutes later gets a fresh reload.
2. **A blocked failure falls through to the deploy poller** (`recoverDuringDeployment`) instead of going silent — it probes the live site every 5s until the deployed commit actually changes, then navigates and shows the "fresh docs" toast. The poller also skips its "is a deploy pending?" GitHub-API gate when assets are known-missing, since that API can be rate-limited or already showing the finished deploy.
3. **Static module-script and stylesheet 404s are now caught too** (capture-phase `error` listener on `/assets/` URLs) — a direct visit on stale cached HTML previously had *no* recovery path at all, because `vite:preloadError` only covers dynamic imports.

Takes effect on ivue.dev once you push and the deploy runs.
